course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.6 key concept: as states expanded and centralized, resistance to state power by Indigenous peoples and others increased
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Pueblo Revolt of 1680
stimulusBlocks.text:
By the 1670s, Pueblo communities in present-day New Mexico had endured decades of Spanish rule. Spanish colonists demanded labor and tribute, and Franciscan missionaries tried to suppress Pueblo religious ceremonies. Drought and raids made life harder still.

In 1680, led by a religious leader named Popé, many Pueblo towns rose together, killed about 400 Spanish colonists and priests, and drove the survivors south out of the region. The Spanish returned in the 1690s, but afterward they generally tolerated more Pueblo religious practice and relied less on forced labor.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect of the Pueblo Revolt?
choices: Pueblo communities converted to Christianity
Spanish rulers increased forced labor and religious suppression afterward
Spanish rulers later tolerated more Pueblo religious practice
Spain never returned to New Mexico
questions.explanation: After returning in the 1690s, the Spanish allowed more Pueblo practice.
choiceExplanations: The revolt defended Pueblo religion.
Spain relied less on forced labor.
After returning in the 1690s, the Spanish allowed more Pueblo practice.
Spain returned in the 1690s.
questions.distinguisher: The passage says Spain relied less on forced labor after returning.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.6 key concept: as states expanded and centralized, resistance to state power increased, from elites, peasants, and rival groups
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing challenges to state power in three regions, c. 1620–1700
stimulusBlocks.text:
In west-central Africa, Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba resisted Portuguese expansion from the 1620s to the 1660s, combining diplomacy, warfare, and alliances with the Dutch. In France, nobles and Paris officials rose against the young Louis XIV in the Fronde between 1648 and 1653. In India, the Maratha leader Shivaji built an independent kingdom in the 1670s and fought the Mughal Empire.

The causes differed. Nzinga resisted a foreign colonial power, the Fronde opposed the growth of royal authority, and the Marathas challenged an empire they saw as foreign and burdensome.

questions.prompt: The Fronde is best understood in the context of
choices: Mughal expansion into the Deccan
declining royal power that left the nobles of France unchallenged
growing royal power that threatened the privileges of nobles
Spanish colonial expansion in the Americas
questions.explanation: Nobles and officials resisted the growth of royal authority.
choiceExplanations: The Mughals were unrelated.
Royal power was growing.
Nobles and officials resisted the growth of royal authority.
The Fronde was a French domestic conflict.
questions.distinguisher: Nobles revolted because royal power was growing, not declining.

questions.prompt: Which cause of the Pueblo Revolt does the passage emphasize?
choices: A shortage of food caused by a drought across the region
A Spanish decision to end all trade with the Pueblo villages
Competition with neighboring peoples for the same horses
Tribute, forced labor, and suppression of Pueblo religion
questions.explanation: The passage describes tribute and labor demands and punishment of traditional religious practices.
choiceExplanations: The passage does not mention drought.
The passage describes Spanish demands, not an end of trade.
The passage does not mention a dispute over horses.
The passage describes tribute and labor demands and punishment of traditional religious practices.
questions.distinguisher: Pueblo communities did face hardships, but the passage names Spanish policies as the cause.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.6 key concept: Indigenous peoples resisted colonial rule, and some revolts forced changes in colonial policy
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Pueblo Revolt, 1680–1692
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1680 the Pueblo peoples of what is now New Mexico rose against Spanish rule. For decades Spanish authorities and Franciscan missionaries had forced Pueblo communities to pay tribute in goods and labor and had punished traditional religious practices such as dances and kachina ceremonies. A religious leader named Popé organized the Pueblo villages, which spoke different languages, and runners carried knotted cords to coordinate the date of the revolt.

Pueblo forces killed about 400 Spaniards, including many priests, and drove the survivors south to El Paso. The Spanish did not retake the region until 1692, and when they did, they allowed Pueblo communities more religious freedom than before.

questions.prompt: The use of knotted cords to coordinate the revolt shows that
choices: the Spanish had given the Pueblo peoples a written alphabet
the revolt was organized by a single government with a central capital
Pueblo leaders used their own signals to unite separate villages
the Pueblo peoples had adopted Spanish military tactics
questions.explanation: Runners carried knotted cords to set the date of the revolt across villages that did not share a language.
choiceExplanations: The passage describes cords, not a written alphabet.
The passage says a religious leader organized separate villages.
Runners carried knotted cords to set the date of the revolt across villages that did not share a language.
The passage does not say the Pueblo peoples used Spanish tactics.
questions.distinguisher: Popé organized the villages, but they were not a single state under one government.
